## Predicates

\

$p$: \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_ ate cereal for breakfast.

\

To apply the statement to many students, define a _Predicate_.

\

*   $P(x)$: $x$ ate cereal for breakfast.

*   $x$ can be _instantiated_ to a particular student, or an arbitrary one.

*   $P(\underline{\hspace{2em}})$ is a proposition.

## One predicate, many rows {.activity}

$P(x)$: cereal $x$ has at least 4 units of protein.

\

Fill in the truth value for each row:

| cereal | protein | $P(x)$ |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| All-Bran | 4 | |
| Froot Loops | 1 | |
| Cheerios | 6 | |
| Trix | 1 | |

\

What kind of object is the last column? \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

## Boolean Masks {.activity}

Select all cereals with at least 4 units of protein and no more than 6 units of sugars.

```{pyodide}
#| setup: true
#| exercise: ex_cereal
import pandas as pd
cereals = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/UBC-CS/dsci220/refs/heads/main/data/cereal.csv')
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_cereal
p = cereals['protein'] < 4
q = cereals['sugars'] > 6
filtered_df = cereals[______]
filtered_df
```

```{pyodide}
#| exercise: ex_cereal
#| check: true
correct_answer = cereals[(cereals['protein'] >= 4) & (cereals['sugars'] <= 6)]
ok = (
    len(filtered_df) == len(correct_answer)
    and filtered_df.index.equals(correct_answer.index)
)
feedback = {"correct": True, "message": "Correct."} if ok else {
    "correct": False, "message": "Use both conditions: protein >= 4 and sugars <= 6."}
feedback
```

## A claim about the data {.activity}

\

> Every cereal with at least 4 units of protein has at most 6 units of sugars.

\

True or false?

\

How would you establish it? \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

{{< countdown minutes=4 >}}

## Two ways to settle it

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Check every row**

```{.python}
(~p | q).all()
```

Returns `True`: settled.
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Find one row that fails**

```{.python}
cereals[p & ~q].head(1)
```

Returns a row: settled.
:::
:::::

\

Written in logic:

$$\forall x\, \big(P(x) \rightarrow Q(x)\big) \qquad\qquad \exists x\, \big(P(x) \wedge \neg Q(x)\big)$$

::: notes
The dataset is finite, so `.all()` checks every case. That is a proof. One
counterexample refutes. Do not editorialize; just let them see that the pandas
call and the quantifier are the same statement.
:::

## Now change one thing {.activity}

\

Same claim, but about **every cereal ever manufactured**.

\

Does `.all()` still settle it? \_\_\_\_\_\_

Does one counterexample still settle it? \_\_\_\_\_\_

\

What could you do instead? \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

{{< countdown minutes=4 >}}

::: notes
Refutation survives; verification does not. When the domain is too big to
enumerate you sample, and the verdict changes from settled to supported. That
is claim B from lecture 1, and it is the rest of their degree.
:::

## Logical Equivalence

\

Ex: Is it true that $(p \lor q) \equiv (q\lor p)$ ?

\

*   $\equiv$ means _logically equivalent_

*   The answer had better be \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_!!!

*   How can we justify our instinct?

::: notes
1. Show same truth table. 2. Chains of equivalence. Same as saying "write a proof".
:::

## Back to the mask {.activity}

::: small-font-size
"at least 4 units of protein and no more than 6 units of sugars"

$p$: a cereal has less than 4 units of protein

$q$: a cereal has more than 6 units of sugars

We suspect $\neg p\wedge \neg q \equiv \neg( p\lor q)$:
:::

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="45%"}
| $p$ | $q$ | $\neg p\wedge \neg q$ |
|-----|-----|----------------------:|
| F   | F   |                       |
| F   | T   |                       |
| T   | F   |                       |
| T   | T   |                       |
:::

::: {.column width="10%"}
:::

:::: {.column width="45%"}
| $p$ | $q$ | $\neg( p\lor q)$ |
|-----|-----|-----------------:|
| F   | F   |                  |
| F   | T   |                  |
| T   | F   |                  |
| T   | T   |                  |
::::
:::::::

::: notes
Half the room does the left table, half the right, then read aloud.
:::

## Where it breaks {.activity}

Add a cereal whose protein is missing.

```{.python}
cereals.loc[len(cereals)] = {'name': 'Mystery', 'protein': None, 'sugars': 3}
p = cereals['protein'] < 4
q = cereals['sugars'] > 6
((~p) & (~q)).sum(), (~(p | q)).sum()
```

\

De Morgan held in the truth table. Do the two counts agree? \_\_\_\_\_\_

Why? \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

::: notes
Missing data gives a third value. Two-valued laws are not guaranteed. Connects
back to lecture 2: a proposition is True or False --- `NaN` is neither, so it
is not one.
:::
